Q134283869.summary: Carved around this small ivory box is a continuous frieze of figures in deep relief. In one view a youthful Christ with a cross-nimbus strides forward, his right hand raised, followed by bearded apostles; in another, a veiled woman kneels under an arched canopy while other women and men approach in animated movement. Such pyxides, used to hold incense or the Eucharistic bread, carried scenes of Christ's healing miracles as reminders of his power to restore body and soul.
facts: The museum's own label (as recorded in the photographer's file names) titles it a pyx with Christ performing miracle healing, Eastern Mediterranean, c. 500.
Q134283869.notes: Inventory Kg 54:214 (old no. 698). Wikidata label misspells 'Wunderheiligungen'. The individual healing scenes (e.g. which miracles are shown) were not identified from a reliable source and are described only generally. Date from the label photographed in Commons; Wikidata gives 6th century.

cur:objects-murano-diptych.summary: This five-part ivory leaf, used as the cover of a gospel book, sets a bearded Christ enthroned beneath an arch at its centre, flanked by two standing apostles. Narrow side panels with standing figures and small narrative scenes surround him, and the lowest band shows the story of Jonah cast into the sea and swallowed by the great fish, the Old Testament sign of the Resurrection; above, two flying angels carry a wreath with a cross. The whole composition proclaims Christ as the enthroned Lord of the Church, framed by his deeds and by prophecy.
facts: It is known as the 'Murano Diptych' and is displayed in the ivory room of the Museo Nazionale in Ravenna; the museum's attribution, as recorded with the photographs, is 'perhaps Egyptian', about 500–550.
Five-part ivory covers of this kind, with a large central panel surrounded by four narrow panels, were a prestigious form of gospel-book binding in the 5th and 6th centuries (type).

cur:objects-murano-diptych.notes: Only one leaf survives in Ravenna. Detailed identification of every small side scene could not be verified from an accessible museum record.
